title: Port Reference
subtitle: The most common network ports in SOC reports — what each one does, and when it's actually worth a second look.

intro.text: A quick reference to check during alert triage, instead of looking up which service runs on which port every single time. The ones marked "seen in the lab" genuinely showed up in an exercise or investigation in this lab — the rest is the set any SOC analyst ends up memorizing from sheer repetition.

intro.title: How to use this in Discover
intro.text: Any port on this list can be searched directly in Threat Hunting/Discover with data.dest_port: 445 (or whichever number) — combine with agent.name or data.src_ip to narrow the result.

blocks.text: Seeing these ports active — especially receiving a connection from outside the network with no known business reason — is a sign to investigate before dismissing.

rows: IRC — historically used as a botnet C2 channel

blocks.title: The general rule, beyond the list
blocks.text: Any unusually high port (above 10000), receiving an inbound connection from outside, with no documented service running there, is suspicious by default — it doesn't need to be on any list to deserve a look.

blocks.title: "Normal" ports hide attacks too
blocks.text: DNS (53) and ICMP are the two classic examples of a legitimate protocol abused as an exfiltration/C2 channel — a port simply being open isn't the only signal; unusual traffic volume on those ports (like in the STUN exercise, where volume confirmed a real video call) also deserves attention when it strays from the expected pattern.
